tldr: By embedding just 20 tokens directly into a VLA policy and applying 3D Gaussian reconstruction and future prediction only during training, this method achieves highly accurate and robust robotic manipulation without slowing down inference.
hero_caption: Taxonomy of robot control policies. While traditional methods rely on 2D images or run heavy 3D and generative models during inference, the proposed method (far right) embeds just 20 World Tokens into the VLA. It employs an asymmetric design that guides 3D structure and future dynamics using Gaussian representations strictly at training time.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies leverage large-scale vision-language pretraining to excel at following instructions. However, learning via action imitation alone struggles to capture metric 3D structure and short-horizon physical evolution. To address this, approaches incorporating 3D depth information or world models predicting future video or latent dynamics have been explored. Yet, these methods often incur heavy computational costs during inference, or produce predicted images that fail to align with physically accurate 3D geometry.

Prior work, GaussianDream, introduced an asymmetric design that uses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS: a technique representing 3D space with tiny Gaussian ellipsoids) as an auxiliary supervisory signal during training, discarding the decoder at inference. Nevertheless, it required a dedicated module to extract 1,024 dense geometric prefixes that had to be retained even during inference, leading to computational overhead and entangled representations. To overcome these issues, GaussianDream++ introduces a streamlined architecture that directly inserts just 20 tokens (16 for state, 4 for prediction) into the VLA backbone (PaliGemma). During training, it reconstructs the current world and predicts future evolution over shared Gaussian primitives, factorizing static and dynamic regions. At inference, the 3DGS decoder and renderer are entirely removed, leaving only the 20 tokens to directly pass 3D geometric context to the Action Expert.

In experiments, the method achieved a 98.6% success rate on the LIBERO simulation benchmark and 87.8% on LIBERO-Plus, showing strong robustness against camera and layout shifts. Furthermore, real-robot experiments demonstrated a dramatic boost in average success from 29.2% (reproduced $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline) to 52.5%, proving high-precision control with only 44 ms of additional latency.
contributions: Designed an ultra-compact 3D world representation using just 20 World Tokens (16 for state, 4 for prediction) inserted directly into the VLA backbone (PaliGemma).

Coupled current world reconstruction with future prediction over shared Gaussian primitives, using static-dynamic factorization to focus learning on physically plausible, interaction-relevant changes.
Established an efficient asymmetric architecture where 3DGS decoding, rendering, and dedicated geometry extraction are strictly training-only, leaving only lightweight token processing at inference.
Demonstrated superior zero-shot robustness against camera and layout shifts on LIBERO-Plus, as well as a substantial success rate improvement (from 29.2% to 52.5%) on a real dual-arm robot.

sections.heading: How to teach VLAs 3D physics while keeping them fast and light
sections.summary: Current VLAs rely on 2D image features and action imitation, struggling with contact-rich 3D manipulation and predicting short-horizon physical changes. Prior work GaussianDream addressed this via Gaussian prediction during training, but still required 1,024 dense external geometric tokens during inference. GaussianDream++ integrates just 20 tokens directly into the model, achieving both full lightweight execution and deep geometric understanding.
sections.details:
While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies that follow language instructions have advanced rapidly, behavior cloning alone faces a fundamental challenge: it struggles to capture the metric 3D structure necessary for contact and grasping, as well as the immediate physical evolution caused by manipulation. Existing studies have explored adding geometric inputs such as depth and point clouds, or employing world models that predict future RGB frames and latent states. However, adding geometry is often limited to understanding static current scenes, while world models carry heavy computational burdens at deployment and their predicted images often fail to match physically accurate geometric changes.

In contrast, prior work GaussianDream adopted a clever asymmetric setup using 3D Gaussian Splatting: it reconstructs and predicts current and future 3D states only during training, discarding the decoders at inference. Even so, GaussianDream generated 1,024 dense queries using dedicated external modules (VGGT and TGE) and fed them into the policy during inference, still relying on an external geometry pipeline with a massive token footprint.

GaussianDream++ fully integrates this world representation into the VLA's vision-language backbone in a native manner. Specifically, it inserts a total of 20 tokens—16 World State Tokens for the current scene and 4 World Prediction Tokens for immediate future changes—and supervises them by decoding 3D Gaussians with a lightweight head strictly during training. At inference, no extra external modules are needed. The 20 tokens inside the backbone directly condition the Action Expert, simultaneously achieving outstanding inference efficiency and strong robustness.

sections.heading: Evolution of geometry-enhanced VLAs, world models, and 3DGS integration
sections.summary: Research enhancing VLA geometry has focused mainly on grounding the current static frame, while future-predicting world models struggle with computational cost and physical consistency. Training-time supervision via 3DGS bridges these paradigms. This work builds on the strengths of GaussianDream while pushing forward token compactness and internal architectural integration.
sections.details:
- **VLA Policies and Geometric Grounding**: Prominent VLAs such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and $\pi_{0.5}$ possess strong vision-language semantic features, but learn metric 3D geometry only indirectly. Methods incorporating point clouds, depth, or 4D features (e.g., G3VLA, VGA) have been proposed; however, these focus primarily on geometrically anchoring the current observation frame and provide insufficient supervision for the short-horizon physical evolution after contact occurs.

- **Predictive Policies and World Models**: Beyond action imitation, approaches predicting future observations, trajectories, or video latents (e.g., Fast-WAM, Cosmos Policy) equip action learning with temporal priors. However, predictions in RGB or latent space frequently break down physically during millimeter-level contact and grasping, despite looking plausible. Moreover, rolling out generative models during inference burdens the control loop.

- **Gaussian World Modeling in Robot Learning**: 3DGS—with explicit position, rotation, scale, opacity, and color—enables differentiable rendering and seamlessly couples geometry with appearance. Prior work GaussianDream used this for auxiliary training tasks, introducing dense self-supervision via RGB, depth, and 3D scene flow. GaussianDream++ inherits this excellent principle of training-time supervision, but critically departs from it by discarding external dense prefix generation and restructuring the representation into compact internal VLA tokens.

sections.heading: How just 20 tokens learn 3D present and future dynamics
sections.summary: Sixteen state tokens and four prediction tokens are added to the input of PaliGemma. A lightweight head reconstructs the current world and predicts future changes from shared 3D Gaussians only during training. Static-dynamic factorization prevents background artifacts and isolates physical changes. At inference, the decoder and renderer are discarded, leaving only the 20 tokens to generate actions quickly.
sections.details:
### 3.1 & 3.2 Policy-Native World Representation and Token Formulation
In GaussianDream++, alongside multi-view observations $o_t$ and language instruction $\ell$, two sets of learnable tokens are inserted directly into the PaliGemma backbone: 16 World State Tokens ($Z^S$) capturing current scene geometry, and 4 World Prediction Tokens ($Z^P$) responsible for short-horizon future prediction. Together, they total just 20 tokens, which are contextualized with image and language tokens via self-attention inside the backbone. The resulting representations are directly fed into the flow-matching Action Expert, conditioning action generation without intermediate projection layers.

### 3.3 Current World Reconstruction
Only during training, a lightweight World Representation Head decodes the state token features into dense Gaussian feature maps. It decouples geometry and appearance into separate prediction branches: the geometry branch predicts depth, which is unprojected using camera intrinsics and extrinsics to determine the 3D Gaussian centers. A stop-gradient is applied to prevent appearance features from corrupting geometry learning, avoiding geometric distortion caused by fitting textures. Metric 3D geometry is enforced on the state tokens by computing reconstruction losses against ground-truth RGB, depth, and opacity.

### 3.4 Coupled Future Prediction
For future prediction, the model inherits the Gaussian primitives constructed for the current world (such as scales and appearance) as a shared template, predicting only the displacement of each Gaussian center ($\Delta \mu$) using prediction tokens and time embeddings. Furthermore, a gating mechanism factorizes static and dynamic regions, penalizing unnecessary motion in background or fixed areas that are static in ground-truth data. This allows the predictive model to concentrate its capacity exclusively on interaction-relevant regions, such as the robot arm and manipulated objects.

### 3.5 Asymmetric Training and Inference
The overall training loss combines the flow-matching action loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}$ with the current reconstruction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{curr}}$ and prediction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}$ using weighting factors. At inference, the 3DGS decoding head, differentiable renderer, and auxiliary loss pipeline are completely stripped away. When controlling the robot, only the 20 tokens are processed within PaliGemma. Action generation directly benefits from representations imbued with 3D geometry and dynamics without any online 3D rollout computation.

sections.heading: Proven robustness and inference efficiency in simulation and real-robot trials
sections.summary: The model achieved 98.6% on the LIBERO benchmark and 87.8% on LIBERO-Plus under unseen perturbations, showing standout resilience against camera and layout shifts. On a real dual-arm robot, it nearly doubled the success rate from 29.2% to 52.5%, adding a mere 44 ms of inference latency.
sections.details:
### 4.1 & 4.2 Simulation Evaluation (LIBERO & LIBERO-Plus)
Across the four task suites of standard LIBERO (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long), GaussianDream++ achieved an average success rate of 98.6%. Furthermore, on LIBERO-Plus, which benchmarks zero-shot robustness against environmental perturbations, it scored 87.8% overall, consistently outperforming GaussianDream (87.0%) and the reproduced $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline (85.5%). Gains were particularly prominent under geometric perturbations: camera shifts improved by +6.9 points over $\pi_{0.5}$ (73.2% to 80.1%), and layout shifts improved by +2.3 points (87.7% to 90.0%). This demonstrates that accurate 3D structure is successfully retained within the tokens despite viewpoint and arrangement changes.

### 4.3 Real-Robot Experiments
Using a real dual-arm robot, the method was evaluated on two tasks: "Bowl-Proximity" (pushing a bowl next to another without tipping it over, requiring millimeter-level precision) and "Eggplant-to-Pink-Plate" (picking an eggplant among distractors and placing it on a pink plate, a multi-step task). Each task was tested under three conditions (Normal, Layout shift, Camera shift) across 20 trials each. The overall average success rate jumped dramatically from 29.2% with the reproduced $\pi_{0.5}$ to 52.5% (+23.3 points), demonstrating strong resilience against viewpoint and layout variations in real environments.

### 4.4 & 4.5 Qualitative Analysis and Inference Efficiency
Visualizing the RGB and depth decoded by the training head showed that, despite originating from coarse token representations, the arm poses and 3D spatial relations of tabletop objects were accurately reconstructed. The future predictions also cleanly captured primary physical movements. In inference latency benchmarks, GaussianDream++ took 330 ms per action chunk compared to 286 ms for $\pi_{0.5}$, adding only 44 ms (a factor of ~1.15). Compared to GaussianDream, which ran 1,024 prefixes and a geometry extractor at runtime, this method is significantly lighter and easier to deploy.

### 4.6 Ablation Studies
Adding tokens without Gaussian training supervision yielded an 86.3% success rate on LIBERO-Plus, showing that 3DGS supervision is vital for performance gains. Removing metric depth loss dropped the overall score from 87.8% to 86.9% (with Camera robustness plunging from 80.1% to 76.5%), while omitting 3D scene flow degraded robustness against noise and layout shifts. This confirms that current geometric constraints and future kinematic constraints work in balanced synergy.

sections.heading: Embedding 3D physical intuition into policies without deploying heavy world models
sections.summary: GaussianDream++ combines just 20 tokens inside a VLA backbone with training-time Gaussian supervision to deliver high precision and robust manipulation. Because it enhances 3D awareness without running external world models or renderers during deployment, it serves as a highly practical recipe for future robot foundation models.
sections.details:
GaussianDream++ shows that the benefits of explicit 3D world modeling can be internalized into VLA policies in the most efficient manner for contact-rich and spatial manipulation tasks. Rather than deploying large 3D or video generative models during inference, its asymmetric philosophy—providing dense geometric and motion supervision via 3DGS during training while keeping only 20 internal tokens at inference—proves exceptionally compelling for compute-constrained robot hardware.

Its high perturbation tolerance in simulation and doubled success rate on a real dual-arm robot (29.2% to 52.5%) clearly substantiate the value of this lightweight formulation. It establishes a practical blueprint for endowing robots with 3D spatial grounding and adaptive anticipation of immediate physical changes without relying on costly online simulators.

takeaways: Re-demonstrated the power of asymmetric architectures: supervise heavily with a 3D world model during training, then discard it to leave only lightweight tokens at inference.
Sharing a current-world template, restricting future prediction to displacements (residuals), and gating static regions is a highly effective way to curb computation and noise.
Pre-supervision using metric depth and 3D scene flow provides robust resilience against common real-world perturbations like camera shifts and initial layout changes.
limitations: Performance on the "Robot shift" condition (adapting to different robot arms) in LIBERO-Plus was lower than baseline $\pi_{0.5}$, showing that generalizing across substantially different embodiments remains a challenge.
Decoding 3D Gaussians and running differentiable rendering during training increases training time and GPU memory usage compared to standalone policy imitation.
The current and future 3D reconstructions derived from World Tokens remain coarse geometric representations, falling short of photorealistic fidelity for fine object boundaries or intricate textures.
